common_name: Victoria Elderberry (Kentville Nova Scotia Research Station American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or rooted-cutting stock in spring into moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bred as a companion pollinator for Ranch and sets a noticeably heavier crop when a second cultivar is planted within 60 feet.

directions: Victoria was released in 1957 from the Kentville Research Station in Nova Scotia as a seedling of Adams No. 2, part of the same Canadian breeding program that produced Kent, Nova, Scotia, and Johns. It ripens mid-season, later than Nova but around the same time as Kent, with medium-sized purple-black berries whose skin is lighter than Kent's or Nova's while the juice inside remains intensely dark purple. Victoria tolerates the shorter, cooler growing seasons of higher latitudes better than many American cultivars and performs well in the partial shade of a woodland-edge planting. It is a proven cross-pollinator for Ranch, and interplanting with any second cultivar improves fruit set and cluster size over a solid block planting.
sources: Kentville Research and Development Centre, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

common_name: Berry Hill Elderberry (Lewis Hill Vermont Alkaline-Soil-Tolerant American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates alkaline soil better than most Sambucus canadensis selections and benefits from a second cultivar such as its companion release Coomer planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Berry Hill was developed in Vermont by nurseryman and author Lewis Hill and is among the most vigorous and cold-hardy of the named American elderberries, ripening its large, deep-red berries early and uniformly across the cluster. Its spreading, decumbent flower cymes are held lower and more horizontally than upright cultivars, which some growers find offers a degree of natural protection from bird predation. Berry Hill is notably the most alkaline-soil-tolerant Sambucus canadensis selection commonly available, making it a good choice on neutral-to-limey garden soils where other elderberry cultivars struggle. It pairs well with its Vermont-bred companion cultivar Coomer for cross-pollination and a staggered but still early harvest window.
sources: Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA)

common_name: Coomer Elderberry (Lewis Hill Vermont Large-Fruited American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; more upright than its spreading companion cultivar Berry Hill, and the two were bred together in Vermont to ripen in the same window for easy combined harvest and cross-pollination.

directions: Coomer is one of two elderberry cultivars developed in Vermont by Lewis Hill, distinguished from its companion release Berry Hill by a more upright growth habit and large, deep-purple-black berries borne in showy clusters. Coomer and Berry Hill were selected to flower and fruit on a similar schedule, making the pair a practical combination for growers who want simultaneous, easy-to-manage harvests along with reliable cross-pollination. As with all American elderberry, cook the berries before eating and expect vigorous root suckering that should be thinned annually to keep the shrub in a defined form. Coomer performs well in the cooler, moist growing conditions of the northern United States and tolerates the partial shade of a woodland edge.

common_name: Goodbarn Elderberry (Elwyn Meader New Hampshire Chance-Seedling American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; reported to be self-fertile and can bear a crop on its own, though yields improve with a second nearby elderberry cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Goodbarn originated as a chance seedling discovered growing under the barn eaves of noted plant breeder Elwyn Meader in Rochester, New Hampshire, and was later named and introduced for its unusual hardiness and vigor. It is among the smallest and shortest-statured named American elderberry cultivars, making it a good option for smaller home gardens, and blooms heavily to set large, evenly ripening annual crops of smaller berries. Goodbarn is notably cold-hardy, tolerating conditions as far north as USDA zone 3, and appears self-fertile, though interplanting with another cultivar is still recommended for maximum fruit set. Cook the berries before eating, as with all elderberry.
sources: Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA)
